analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it with payroll taxes on high earners' income above the cap.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise Social Security benefits and fund them by phasing in Social Security taxes on earnings above the annual cap was referred to two House committees on June 23, 2026 and has not moved since; Congress is still in session.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill does two things. First, it increases Social Security checks: it raises the share of a low earner's wages counted toward benefits, raises the dollar amount of earnings that gets the most generous treatment, counts a slice of high earners' above-cap earnings toward their benefits, boosts the benefit formula over time, recalculates benefits for people already retired so they get the increase too, and switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to an inflation index built for retirees' spending, which weighs health care costs more heavily. Second, it pays for that by phasing out the ceiling on wages subject to Social Security tax: income above the annual cap would be 80% taxable in 2026, less each year, and fully taxable by 2030, for employees, employers, and the self-employed alike.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries, especially those with lower lifetime earnings, who would see larger monthly checks, a benefit increase applied retroactively to people already retired, and cost-of-living adjustments keyed to retiree spending patterns rather than the general inflation index.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees and disabled beneficiaries, especially lower earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the percentage factor for the lowest portion of a worker's counted earnings from 90% to 95%, which increases benefits most for people with smaller lifetime earnings.

Raises the first bend point to $6,300 and then increases it by 1 percentage point per year starting in 2031, reaching 15% above the 2026 level by 2045, so the most generous part of the benefit formula covers more earnings over time.

Requires the Social Security Commissioner to recompute benefits for people already on the rolls using the higher bend point, and guarantees nobody's recomputed benefit can come out lower than what they were receiving.

Creates a 'surplus earnings' credit: 5% of a worker's earnings above the annual payroll tax cap count toward their benefit for people becoming eligible after 2030, so high earners who pay the new taxes get a partial benefit credit back.

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers that the Bureau of Labor Statistics would publish, reflecting the spending patterns of people at early retirement age, where health care weighs more heavily than in the general index.

Pays for the expansion by making wages above the annual contribution and benefit base progressively taxable for Social Security purposes: 80% in 2026, then 20 percentage points less each year, reaching 0% excluded by 2030, applying to employees, employers, and self-employment income.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and the self-employed whose income exceeds the annual Social Security tax cap, plus the businesses that employ them, who would pay the employer share on that income as well. The taxes phase in gradually, but by 2030 earnings above the cap would be fully taxed at the 12.4% combined rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

drawbacks.text: High earners would face a new tax on income above the annual cap, and employers of highly paid workers would owe the matching share, which critics argue discourages work and hiring at the top and raises costs for businesses that pay high salaries.

The bill partially offsets the new taxes for high earners by crediting 5% of their above-cap earnings toward their future benefits, which returns some of the new revenue to the people paying the most and slightly dilutes the redistribution toward lower earners.

Cost-of-living adjustments based on an elderly-specific price index would likely grow faster over time than the current index, which increases the program's long-term cost even as the new taxes strengthen its finances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are real, broad, and weighted toward people with lower benefits, and they are paired with a funding mechanism that phases in over five years rather than borrowing. The main honest objections are the new tax burden on a small group of high earners and their employers, and the fact that the more generous inflation index adds long-term cost on top of the expansion. On balance the trade is straightforward: a larger, more secure benefit for tens of millions of retirees, paid for by taxing income that is currently exempt above roughly the top 5-6% of earners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce committees, and neither committee has taken it up; Congress is still in session, so it is sitting, not dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-CA) introduced the bill on June 23, 2026, and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and Workforce.
Four Democratic cosponsors joined; no other action, hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened yet, the status quo holds: high earners continue to pay no Social Security tax above the annual cap, and beneficiaries continue receiving benefits under the current formula.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners keep the cap; benefits stay the same

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise Social Security benefits funded by taxing earnings above the payroll tax cap.

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill.

against.role: Primary committee of referral for Social Security tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 23, 2026 and has held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received a split referral on June 23, 2026 and has taken no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, so the partisan split is untested; all five supporters in the record are Democrats, and the committees that have not acted are chaired by Republicans.

industries.industry: High earners above the Social Security payroll tax cap
industries.note: Income above the annual cap is currently exempt from the 12.4% Social Security tax; the bill phases that exemption out entirely by 2030, so the households collecting the highest wages would pay thousands more per year. In exchange they get a small benefit credit, but far less than the tax they pay.

Self-employment income above the cap would be taxed under the same phase-in, so high-earning consultants, partners, and small-business owners face the full combined tax on excess earnings with no employer to split it with.
Employers owe the matching share of Social Security tax on wages above the cap under the bill's tax-code changes, raising labor costs for firms with highly compensated staff.

The agency would take on new work, including recomputing benefits for all current beneficiaries and publishing an elderly-specific price index with BLS, with sums authorized to be appropriated for that purpose.

analysis.trajectory: At this stage, with a Democratic sponsor, four cosponsors, no Republican support in the record, and no committee action months before the Congress ends, the bill's likely path is the usual one for a first-term member's expansion bill: no markup in Ways and Means, and it expires in January unless its provisions get attached to a larger package.
